notes.trap: `any(...)` ignores NULLs, but if every input is NULL, or there are no rows, it returns NULL rather than false. Wrap it in `coalesce(...)` if you need a strict boolean.
notes.example_sql: SELECT any(col) FROM VALUES (CAST(NULL AS BOOLEAN)), (CAST(NULL AS BOOLEAN)) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: With a single non-null value, `stddev_samp(...)` returns NULL, not 0.0 and not NaN, because the sample size minus one is zero. `stddev_pop(...)` returns 0.0 for the same input.
notes.example_sql: SELECT stddev_samp(col) FROM VALUES (5) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: Unlike `var_samp(...)`, `var_pop(...)` of a single value returns 0.0 rather than NULL. The result is always DOUBLE, even for integer input.
notes.example_sql: SELECT var_pop(col) FROM VALUES (7) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: `min(...)` compares using the column type, so on strings it is lexicographic. The string '10' sorts before '9', so cast to a numeric type first if the values are numbers stored as text.
notes.example_sql: SELECT min(col) FROM VALUES ('10'), ('9') AS tab(col)

notes.trap: `mode(...)` ignores NULLs entirely, even when NULL is the most frequent value. The result is the most frequent non-null value, or NULL only if all inputs are NULL.
notes.example_sql: SELECT mode(col) FROM VALUES (CAST(NULL AS INT)), (NULL), (NULL), (1) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: By default `last_value(...)` does not skip NULLs, so a trailing NULL row makes the result NULL. Pass true as the second argument to ignore NULLs. Without an ORDER BY in a window, the result depends on row order and is non-deterministic.
notes.example_sql: SELECT last_value(col) FROM VALUES (10), (5), (NULL) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: A grouping key that is itself NULL looks the same as a ROLLUP/CUBE subtotal row. Only `grouping(...)` = 1 marks the real subtotal; a group whose key is NULL still has `grouping(...)` = 0.
notes.example_sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT grouping(k) AS g FROM VALUES (1), (NULL) AS t(k) GROUP BY ROLLUP(k)) WHERE g = 0

notes.trap: The argument order is (y, x), with the dependent variable first. Any row where either y or x is NULL is dropped from the whole computation, so a NULL in x also removes that row's y value.
notes.example_sql: SELECT regr_syy(y, x) FROM VALUES (1, 2), (2, null), (2, 3), (2, 4) AS tab(y, x)
